item.title: Case Study: French Kitchenware Brand Cut Aluminum Utensil Costs by 32%
item.description: This is the full playbook of a real engagement we closed for CuisinePro — a French kitchenware importer with 11 distributors across the EU. Six months ago they were locked into a Guangzhou trading company paying €2.68 per aluminum utensil with a 38% QC reject rate. Today they source directly from a Chaozhou factory at €1.82, with 4% defects, LFGB §31 + CE compliant, privately labeled, and landed DDP Le Havre in 28 days. Every number in this post comes from signed invoices, AQL inspection reports we attended on-site, and our client’s landed-cost ledgers — no estimates, no rounding.

item.title: Supplier Relationship Management China: Tiering Incentives & Risk Diversification
item.description:
Most China buyers treat suppliers as disposable: find the cheapest one place an order repeat until something breaks then find a new one. This transactional approach costs more in the long run — in re-audit expenses quality failures stockouts and lost negotiation leverage.

Supplier Relationship Management (SRM) is the opposite approach: treating your supplier base as a strategic portfolio to be tiered incentivized and diversified. This guide covers the 4-tier supplier classification system the 3 incentive mechanisms that actually work with Chinese factories the risk diversification strategies (single dual and multi-source) and the 5 long-term benefits of building real partnerships. We include a real case study of a client who reduced supply disruption risk by 18% by transitioning from single-source to dual-source.

item.title: China Supplier Evaluation Scorecard: 10-Dimensional Factory Rating Template
item.description:
Every buyer who has sourced from China has faced the same question: “I have 5 quotes. The prices range from 2.10 to 3.80 USD. Which factory do I pick?” Most buyers pick the cheapest one and hope. The smarter ones pick the middle one and pray. The professional buyers use a supplier evaluation scorecard — a structured 10-dimensional rating system that removes emotion and guesswork from the decision.

This guide gives you the complete scorecard we use at Yeatru for every factory evaluation. Each of the 10 dimensions is scored 0–10 with clear scoring criteria you can apply yourself. We include a real case study of a 2026 engagement where we scored 5 factories for a US kitchenware brand and selected the winner — and why the cheapest factory scored dead last. We also describe the downloadable template format so you can replicate it in your own procurement process.

item.title: Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR) for Chinese Factories: Template & Process
item.description:
What Is a Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR)?

A Supplier Corrective Action Request (SCAR) is a formal, documented request that a supplier investigate the root cause of a defect and change its process so the defect cannot recur. It sits inside the wider CAPA system (Corrective and Preventive Action): the corrective action fixes the specific batch, and the preventive action changes the process permanently. A SCAR is triggered when a defect is critical, when a defect rate breaches your AQL 2.5 major standard, or when the same defect reappears across batches — precisely when a one-off rework has already proven insufficient.

item.title: Purchase Order Process China Sourcing: From PO Issue to Delivery SOP
item.description:
A purchase order is the most important document in China sourcing. It is the contract that defines what you are buying how much you pay when it ships and what happens if something goes wrong. Yet 71% of first-time buyers issue a one-line PO (“10 000 pcs silicone spatula at 0.85 USD”) and wonder why the factory delivered a different product.

This guide walks you through the complete 8-step purchase order process that Yeatru uses for every client engagement. Each step includes a checklist and the most common pitfalls. We include a real case study of a 12 000 USD order from PO signature to delivery a payment method comparison and a list of 10 mandatory clauses that every China PO must contain.

item.title: How to Read a China Inspection Report: Sections, Red Flags & How to Challenge It
item.description:
What Is a China Inspection Report?

A China inspection report is the written record a QC inspector produces after physically sampling a production lot at the factory, usually during a pre-shipment inspection (PSI). It states the lot size, the sample size (n) drawn under ISO 2859-1 / ANSI Z1.4, the AQL levels (default 2.5 major / 4.0 minor / 0 critical), the defect count in each class, the accept (Ac) versus reject (Re) comparison, dated photo evidence, and a final Pass / Conditional / Fail verdict. It is a contract deliverable that releases or withholds your balance payment — not a marketing PDF.

item.title: FOB Origin vs FOB Destination: Who Pays Freight & Who Bears Risk
item.description:
What Are FOB Origin and FOB Destination?

FOB Origin and FOB Destination are US domestic shipping terms used in B2B commerce within the United States. They determine who pays the freight carrier and when title (ownership) and risk of loss transfer between buyer and seller. Despite sharing the “FOB” acronym, these are not the same as the Incoterms FOB used for international sea freight.

item.title: FCA vs EXW for China Sourcing: Which to Use & Why
item.description:
What Are FCA and EXW?

EXW (Ex Works) is the Incoterm that places maximum obligation on the buyer. The seller only needs to make the goods available at their factory or warehouse; you arrange and pay for everything from that point: China inland trucking, export clearance, international freight, insurance, import clearance, duty, and last-mile.

item.title: How to Get Factory Direct Pricing in China: Avoid Trading Company Markups
item.description: Every China buyer has seen the price gap: the same silicone spatula quoted at 2.80 USD by one supplier and 4.20 USD by another for the identical spec. The 1.40 USD difference is not quality — it is the trading company markup. The 2.80 USD quote came from the actual Ningbo silicone factory; the 4.20 USD quote came from a Yiwu trading company that buys from that same factory and marks it up.

item.title: ETA vs ETD in China Shipping: What Each Date Means
item.description:
What Do ETA and ETD Mean?

ETD (Estimated Time of Departure) is the date and time a vessel or aircraft is scheduled to leave the origin port or airport — for China sourcing, that means leaving a Chinese port such as Ningbo, Shanghai or Shenzhen (or an airport such as Guangzhou or Hong Kong). ETA (Estimated Time of Arrival) is the date and time it is scheduled to reach the destination port or airport. The two are linked: the carrier calculates the ETA by adding its published transit time to the ETD.

item.title: Eco Regulations China Sourcing: CSRD, CBAM, EU Battery, Prop 65
item.description:
What Are Eco Regulations?

Eco (environmental) regulations are laws that impose environmental obligations on products, their supply chains, or the companies that sell them. Unlike voluntary eco certifications, these are mandatory — non-compliance leads to customs refusal, fines, or product recalls. For China importers, the regulations that matter most are in the destination market (EU and US), but China’s own environmental enforcement also affects factory availability and cost. The key regulations are EU CBAM (carbon border tax), EU CSRD (sustainability reporting), EU Battery Regulation (battery passport), EU Packaging Regulation (recycled content), California Prop 65 (chemical warnings), US TSCA (chemical substances), and China’s dual carbon goals. See also product certifications and eco certifications.

item.title: Eco Certifications China: ISO 14001, FSC, GOTS, GRS
item.description:
What Are Eco Certifications?

Eco (environmental) certifications are third-party-verified labels that prove a product or factory meets environmental standards — responsible forestry, organic fibres, recycled content, chemical safety, energy efficiency, or carbon neutrality. When you source from China, eco certifications matter for three reasons: market access (Amazon, Walmart, EU public procurement require them), brand protection (greenwashing claims need evidence), and regulatory compliance (EU CSRD, CBAM and EPR schemes create mandatory disclosure duties). The most relevant standards for China importers are ISO 14001 (factory environmental management), FSC (wood/paper), GOTS (organic textiles), GRS (recycled content), OEKO-TEX (textile chemicals), EPEAT and Energy Star (electronics). See also product certifications and ethical sourcing.

item.title: Defective Goods from China: Claim, Rework, Replacement & Refund Playbook
item.description:
What Is a Defective-Goods Claim Against a Chinese Supplier?

A defective-goods claim is a formal, documented demand that a Chinese supplier remedy goods that fail your agreed specification after delivery. It is built on three things: evidence taken before the goods are sorted or resold, a defect rate measured against the contract’s AQL 2.5 major / 4.0 minor / 0 critical standard, and a written remedy (rework, replacement, refund or price credit) within the contract’s claim window. A claim is not a complaint — it is a contract action with a number attached.

item.title: DDU vs DDP for China Sourcing: The Difference & Who Pays Duty
item.description:
What Does DDU Mean, and How Does It Differ From DDP?

DDU (Delivered Duty Unpaid) and DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) are both door-to-door shipping arrangements. Under either one the seller arranges export clearance in China, international freight, insurance, and delivery to the buyer’s address. The one difference is import customs clearance and import duty: with DDU the buyer clears customs and pays the duty; with DDP the seller does both.

item.title: DAP vs DDP for China Sourcing: Key Differences & Cost
item.description:
What Are DAP and DDP?

DAP (Delivered at Place) and DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) are the two Incoterms 2020 terms where the seller delivers goods all the way to the buyer’s door. The seller handles export clearance, international freight, insurance, and last-mile delivery. The only difference is who handles import clearance and pays import duty: under DAP it’s the buyer; under DDP it’s the seller.

item.title: CIF vs CIP for China Sourcing: Insurance, Risk & Mode
item.description:
What Are CIF and CIP?

CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) and CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To) are the two Incoterms where the seller pays for both freight and cargo insurance to the destination. The key difference is transport mode:

  • CIF applies to sea and inland waterway transport only. The seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port. Risk transfers when goods are on board the vessel at the port of shipment.
  • CIP applies to any mode of transport (air, sea, road, rail, multimodal). The seller pays freight and insurance to the named destination. Risk transfers when goods are handed to the first carrier.

Think of CIP as the all-modes version of CIF. CIP is the correct term when the journey isn’t purely sea — for example, Yiwu → Shenzhen truck → Hong Kong air → EU, or China → Europe by rail.

item.title: China Procurement Cost Breakdown: The True TCO Beyond Unit Price
item.description:
Most first-time China buyers build their sourcing budget on a single number: the factory’s unit price. They multiply by quantity add a rough guess for freight and call it done. Then the container arrives and the actual invoice is 25–40% higher than expected. The difference is not fraud — it is the cost components that the factory quote deliberately does not include.

This guide breaks down the 6 cost components that make up the true total cost of ownership (TCO) for a China-sourced order: product unit price tooling/sampling certification/testing quality control logistics/freight and duties/taxes. For each component we give the percentage range real dollar amounts and the common traps that inflate it. We close with a full cost breakdown of a real 5 000 USD PO and a comparison table showing how a unit-price-only decision differs from a TCO-based decision.
